history.title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst
history.summary: Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI. On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there. Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it. history.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
history.summary: Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances. Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations. Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. history.title: Spectrum Adaptation of AI-Native Autoencoder Communications with Transfer Learning
history.summary: End-to-end physical-layer learning replaces separate modulation, coding, and detection operations with an autoencoder (AE) that consists of a jointly trained encoder-decoder pair at the transmitter and the receiver. This paper studies AI-native communications with AEs and quantifies the sensitivity to training-test mismatch in channel models. Models trained only on an AWGN channel achieve low bit error rates (BERs) under matched conditions but degrade severely on Rayleigh fading with practical front-end impairments. To reduce the time and energy required to adapt to new channel conditions, we propose a low-latency transfer-learning procedure that starts from an AWGN-pretrained system and fine-tunes only a small subset of transmitter and receiver layers while freezing the remainder. We further formulate layer selection as a budget-constrained optimization problem that identifies the most informative parameters to update during adaptation. This preserves the learned signal geometry and the deep decision structure while adapting lightweight front ends to fading- and impairment-induced mixing. For AE communications, we show that partial updates remove the mismatch-induced error floor and approach the BER of fully retrained models. We provide a layer-wise study and quantify resource-performance trade-offs, showing that modest adaptation substantially reduces BER while cutting training time, multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations, energy consumption, and the fraction of updated parameters for resource-efficient implementation.
history.attribution: Source: arXiv — Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI). Original article linked.

history.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
history.summary: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.

history.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
history.summary: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.
history.attribution: Source: arXiv — Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI). Original article linked.

history.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
history.summary: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $μ$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $μ$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.
history.attribution: Source: arXiv — Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI). Original article linked.

history.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
history.summary: This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios. Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. history.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
history.summary: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

history.title: WebVibe: Multimodal Interactive Website Generation via Reverse Synthesis and Visual Self-Distillation
history.summary: Although multimodal large language models translate single screenshots into static HTML, generating interactive functional websites from design specifications still struggles with multi-page routing and stateful widget transitions. Examining existing training pipelines reveals two bottlenecks: (1) in forward data synthesis (X -> Y), writing the specification X before code execution leaves unimplemented or altered requirements in X as supervision noise; and (2) in reinforcement learning, scalar rewards discard the rich state transitions observed during replay. Based on these findings, we introduce WebVibe and Interactive-SDPO to train InteractiveCoder. WebVibe reverses synthesis into Y -> X by verifying cross-page and in-page interactions in the browser before deriving multimodal inputs from replay-confirmed states to build the 31,542-site WebVibe-32K corpus with reusable execution contracts. Interactive-SDPO then conditions a weight-sharing self-teacher on the replay trace and a 2x2 state-transition montage to provide token-level supervision at zero inference-time overhead. On the public Vision2Web L2, one-shot InteractiveCoder-9B nearly 3x its base model's functional score (20.2 to 55.2 FS) and matches a 1T-parameter coding agent in a single pass with 111x fewer total parameters and 78x fewer tokens. On our WebVibeBench, InteractiveCoder-4B and 9B further outperform all evaluated baselines by over 23 points.

history.title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
history.summary: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

history.title: Latent-in-the-Middle: On the Security of Cross-Model Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
history.summary: As large language models increasingly collaborate in heterogeneous multi-agent systems, latent communication has emerged as an efficient alternative to exchanging natural-language messages. By sharing internal representations, agents can avoid repeatedly processing the same context, reducing communication overhead and prefill computation. One such mechanism is cross-model Key-Value (KV) cache transfer, which uses a learned mapper to translate a source model's KV cache into one a target model can use. However, this handoff means the target model consumes context it did not encode itself, thus calling into question whether its safety alignment still holds. In this work, we investigate the security implications of latent handoffs by introducing Chasm, a framework characterizing cross-model handoff attacks across three new attack surfaces: the source model, mapper, and handoff mechanism itself. Our experiments reveal that latent handoffs substantially undermine safety alignment and prompt-injection defenses. Notably, a target model that follows only 0.4% of benchmark prompt injections natively, follows up to 44.2% when transferred through a mapper from a source model. On the other hand, for jailbreak attacks, transfer alone raises attack success by up to 24.6 pp within a model family and zero-shot attacks by up to 69.2 pp, whereas white-box optimization through the mapper boosts the attack success rate to 92.5%, against 37.5% for ordinary GCG on the same target. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose a lightweight target-side cache guard that corrects transferred caches to restore the target model's refusal, considerably mitigating these attacks.

history.title: LatentCP-DPO: Conformal Pessimism for DPO with Finite-Sample Guarantees
history.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns a response policy from human preference data, but with a limited dataset it can overfit to noisy or weakly informative preference labels. We introduce LatentCP-DPO, a framework that combines conformal prediction with pessimistic preference optimization for Bradley-Terry (BT) pairwise feedback and Plackett-Luce (PL) ranking feedback. Building on LatentCP's construction of uncertainty sets for unobserved model parameters, we address how to incorporate this uncertainty into preference optimization and characterize its effect on policy performance. Under exchangeability and a correctly specified preference model, we construct uncertainty sets for latent relative rewards with finite-sample marginal coverage from conformal prediction sets for observable preferences. We then learn a response policy by maximizing the worst-case expected preference log-likelihood over these uncertainty sets, using an independent collection of prompts and candidate responses without preference labels. Under suitable assumptions, we establish finite-sample upper bounds on regularized policy suboptimality that separate policy-class approximation error, conformal uncertainty, and statistical estimation error. For BT feedback, we further establish a worst-case lower bound for LatentCP-DPO that matches the upper bound's reciprocal dependence on the number of unlabeled optimization examples. The lower bound also shows that the uncertainty sets can induce a bias that persists as the optimization sample grows. Together, these results characterize both the statistical accuracy and potential limitations of preference optimization using conformal uncertainty sets. Experiments support the benefits of the proposed framework in finite preference datasets.

history.title: Teaching Students to Stand on Their Own: Distilling Vision Foundation Models for Fine-Grained Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning
history.summary: Fine-grained few-shot class-incremental learning (FG-FSCIL) aims to incrementally learn visually similar new classes from limited images without catastrophic forgetting. Prior work typically learns strong representations on base classes or leverages vision foundation models (VFMs) directly as backbones or via knowledge distillation. However, VFM backbones incur high computational costs and do not guarantee fine-grained recognition. Although knowledge distillation reduces inference cost, our preliminary experiments reveal that distilled students still lag substantially behind their VFM teachers, particularly on new classes. To address this limitation, we propose STAND, a systematic VFM-to-student distillation design tailored for FG-FSCIL. Specifically, STAND connects the teacher and student by equipping the student with a fixed copy of the teacher's classifier, aligning their outputs via projectors, and feeding both models composite images that combine different training images. On these composite images, relation distillation matches how the teacher and the student relate each image to other images, while difference distillation matches how this relation changes between two composite images. Finally, we freeze the student and classify new classes using length-calibrated prototypes, which restore the reduced similarity of few-shot prototypes. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that STAND achieves state-of-the-art performance across FG-FSCIL datasets at low computational cost, while generalizing across student backbones and broader datasets.

history.title: REFORGE: LLM-Assisted RTL Bug Repair with Structured Context and Verification Feedback
history.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write and repair RTL, but successful compilation or testbench execution does not establish defect removal, behavioral preservation, security, or implementation feasibility. Existing LLM-based RTL repair methods often report a single repair rate without retaining separate evidence for these properties, limiting reproducible comparison and integration into hardware design flows. We present REFORGE, which, to our knowledge, is the first LLM-assisted RTL repair framework that maintains and accumulates structured repair evidence across iterations, allowing it to generate fixes that satisfy multiple objectives simultaneously, including functionality, behavioral equivalence, security, and cost efficiency. REFORGE profiles buggy RTL, identifies structural and security-relevant features, localizes failing behavior, and uses verification-guided diagnosis to generate complete RTL repair variants. Each variant undergoes syntax checking, simulation, formal analysis, off-trigger preservation, security re-scan, and synthesis-based power, performance, and area analysis. We implement REFORGE as a backend-independent repair-and-verification flow and evaluate it in 288 runs across three LLM backends and three benchmark suites. On CirFix, the proposed context and diagnosis increase runs delivering a checked repair from 32/63 to 51/63, while every configuration repairs the Hack@DAC OpenTitan defect. Evidence records also show that a testbench-only criterion reports 3.9 times more repairs than the full set of applicable checks, security-clean outputs may lack functional verification, and different RTL repairs can implement equivalent hardware. These results show that LLM-generated RTL repairs require explicit multi-stage verification evidence rather than a single pass/fail outcome.

history.title: WhatIf: Counterfactual World Models over Action-Grounded Causal Graphs for Robotic Manipulation
history.summary: World models predict what happens under an action, but choosing between actions requires comparing their outcomes in the same physical situation. Factual transitions alone determine action-wise marginal futures and average effects, but not individual effects or the probability that switching actions causes harm. We introduce WhatIf, a counterfactual world model for manipulation that couples candidate futures through shared latent physics and transition noise inferred from factual history. Each candidate action induces a sparse object-factor causal graph describing the physical pathways it activates. Rolling out these graphs under the shared situation anchors predictions to observed outcomes and confines action contrasts to the objects each action reaches. Shared type-conditioned functions support varying numbers of objects, while a round-trip loss enforces action-invariant abduction without counterfactual labels. We show that replacing an individual effect with its conditional mean incurs mean-squared error equal to its conditional variance, motivating comparisons between coupled futures. Building on these comparisons, Counterfactual Advantage Planning (CAP) ranks plans by their advantage over an incumbent within shared situations and constrains the probability of harm. Paired advantages reduce estimator variance by a factor of $1-ρ$, where $ρ$ is the correlation between branch outcomes, and cancel model errors shared by both branches. Each executed transition provides hindsight advantages to update the physics posterior, the next plan, and an amortized policy without a learned critic. We further establish when observational transitions identify interventional dynamics. Paired simulator interventions evaluate counterfactual accuracy, graph recovery, compositional generalization, and decision quality.

history.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
history.summary: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.

history.title: JOVE ICE: Intent Guided Cloud Edge Device Collaboration for AI Glasses
history.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and LLM based agents have expanded the capabilities of AI glasses, enabling egocentric visual question answering, memory retrieval, and proactive assistance. These applications involve diverse inputs, including speech, images, and video, and range from simple device control to complex visual reasoning, posing challenges for efficient computation and communication. While video centric capabilities have received considerable attention, simple text based and device executable tasks remain underexplored despite their prevalence in daily interactions. Efficiently supporting diverse workloads within a unified assistant remains an open challenge. We propose JOVE ICE, an intent guided cloud, edge, and device collaborative framework that routes requests among AI glasses, a paired smartphone, and cloud servers according to user intent. JOVE ICE integrates hierarchical intent classification with dynamic subagent orchestration to select efficient execution paths and flexibly incorporate new applications through specialized subagents. Analysis of real world AI glasses requests reveals that simple device control tasks account for over 30% of interactions, which JOVE ICE handles directly on device to avoid unnecessary cloud computation and costs. Evaluations on three public benchmarks demonstrate that JOVE ICE reduces time to first token by approximately 13% and token usage by over 11% compared with conventional device and cloud architectures, while maintaining task quality. These results demonstrate the potential of intent guided collaboration to improve the efficiency and scalability of AI glasses.

history.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
history.summary: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/

history.title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
history.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.

history.title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
history.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

history.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
history.summary: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

history.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
history.summary: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent

history.title: Benchmarking Evidence Sufficiency in Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
history.summary: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.

history.title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
history.summary: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

history.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
history.summary: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.
history.attribution: Source: arXiv — Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI). Original article linked.

history.title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving
history.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.

history.title: Beyond Expected Value: PPO with Distributional Critics for Systematic Conservation Planning
history.summary: Systematic conservation planning must allocate limited protection budgets sequentially under ecological and climatic uncertainty. Static tools cannot adapt as conditions change, and policies optimised only for expected outcomes can fail on the worst-case trajectories climate change makes increasingly likely. CAPTAIN was the first framework to cast this as sequential reinforcement learning, but its gradient-free Evolution Strategies (ES) optimiser lacks per-timestep credit assignment. We replace ES with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) via a Plackett-Luce solution to CAPTAIN's non-differentiable action space, and replace its scalar critic with an Implicit Quantile Network (IQN) modelling the full return distribution. A matched-granularity comparison shows decision granularity, not the optimiser, drives most of the ecological gain, so the real contribution is training efficiency and extensibility to risk-sensitive objectives. On a New Zealand marine dataset, it matches or exceeds ES's outcomes at a fraction of the training cost, offering a template for future work ES's black-box design could not support

history.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
history.summary: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

history.title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
history.summary: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

history.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
history.summary: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

history.title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
history.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

history.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
history.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

history.title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
history.summary: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.

history.title: RepoEviAgent: Scalable Synthesis of Evidence-Grounded Repository-Level Question Answering Tasks
history.summary: Real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks require agents to understand repository structures, cross-module dependencies, and runtime behaviors, posing significant challenges for constructing high-quality training and evaluation data. To address this, we propose RepoEviAgent, a scalable SWE data construction framework that integrates quality-aware data curation and role-specialized multi-agent task synthesis. Starting from 8,477 open-source repositories and approximately 2.48 million pull request records, we employ semantic alignment, complexity constraints, and multidimensional quality assessment to identify valuable SWE data. We further develop a sandbox-based multi-agent framework that integrates automated environment construction, execution validation, repository exploration, and evidence-grounded Q&A synthesis. Based on this framework, we construct RepoEviQA, a benchmark for Repository-Level Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, comprising 334 tasks across five programming languages and diverse SWE categories, with rigorous rubric-based evaluation. We evaluate five frontier coding models on RepoEviQA, revealing substantial performance differences across task categories and programming languages.

history.title: CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?
history.summary: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work showed that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot shows no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

history.title: No Fixed Configuration Is Best: Context- and Cost-Aware Tuning of LLM Pipelines, with an Application to Schema Matching and Mapping
history.summary: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and where the remaining accuracy is. First, tuning buys cost and a little accuracy. On 35 tasks, with whole groups of tasks held out from tuning, one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy (HR@1) over the default at 18% more cost, and another keeps the accuracy of the default at 32% lower cost. Second, the accuracy depends on a choice that numeric tuning cannot reach. Restricting the search for each source column to one assigned target table changes HR@1 by +30 points on a MIMIC-III to OMOP task and by -52 points on a task built from database views, more than numeric tuning gains on nine of ten test tasks. Neither setting is right for all tasks: on the larger set of 41 tasks used for the remaining results, mean HR@1 is 75.7% with the restriction (the default) and 83.1% without it. Third, choosing the setting per task is not enough either: even an oracle that picks the better setting for each task reaches only 87.8% on the 41 tasks, because the better setting differs between the columns of one task. The pipeline therefore runs both settings, and an LLM judge chooses among their candidate answers on the 26% of columns on which they disagree. This reaches 91.5% HR@1 on the 41 tasks, at 5.9 times the cost of the default, about one cent per column.

history.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Malaria Parasite Detection and Species Differentiation in Thick Blood Smear Images: A Pilot Feasibility Study
history.summary: Species-level differentiation of Plasmodium falciparum (PF) and P. vivax (PV) determines treatment, yet deep learning detectors rarely test whether their explanations are reliable. In this pilot feasibility study of TRACE-Mal, a research prototype combining YOLOv8n-seg detection and a six-model soft-voting ensemble, we examined whether agreement among three post-hoc explanation methods (Grad-CAM, LIME and SHAP) is associated with the correctness of species calls. the study analysed 2,847 parasite crops from 250 thick smears within publicly available Lacuna Malaria Datasets. The model achieved an mAP50 score of 0.79 and the ensemble had a macro F1 of 0.84 (PF recall 0.86; PV recall 0.74). Unadjusted analyses of crops revealed that predictions explained by greather than or equal to 2 methods were more accurate (86.2% vs 78.9%; difference 7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 3.5-11.1) compared to those explained by less than 2 methods. As the number of explanatory methods increased so did prediction accuracy (from 73.8% for no methods to 89.5% for all three methods). When performing a cluster-bootstrap analysis of 60 test images, again there was a positive consensus difference (7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 2.9-11.8). Further, incorporating explanation information into a model's prediction confidence enhanced its error differentiation ability (AUROC 0.024; 95% CI 0.008-0.041). PF and PV parasite crops have distinct morphologies. Although based on one unvalidated public data source, these findings demonstrate proof-of-concept and should not be taken as a measure of diagnostic capability.

history.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
history.summary: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
history.attribution: Source: arXiv — Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI). Original article linked.

history.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
history.summary: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

history.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
history.summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

history.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
history.summary: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

history.title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
history.summary: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

history.title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
history.summary: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

history.title: Replay Before You Reply: Second-Look Prompting for Unified Multimodal Encoding
history.summary: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. We introduce Second-Look Prompting (SLP), a training-free method that repeats the image-question pair in the input. In the repeated copy, every visual and textual token can attend to the complete input, yielding a unified multimodal encoding of the pair. Moreover, the added visual tokens contribute computation beyond re-exposing the image: even a blank image in their place can improve reasoning. Across 12 benchmarks, SLP improves the overall average score of every evaluated model, spanning nine open-source models (3B-72B) and three proprietary frontier models, with gains reaching 5.6 points for Gemini 3 Flash on MATH-Vision. Our analysis reveals two complementary mechanisms: the question guides where the second image attends, and the added visual tokens act as a prefill scratchpad whose hidden states retain answer-relevant information from the image and question. These findings highlight input presentation as a simple yet effective way to improve VLM performance.

history.title: Predicting Rare-Mode Collapse in Recursive Generative Training from Single-Generation Calibration
history.summary: Recursive generative training can preserve sample counts in a rare region while silently eroding its characteristic core. Mapping this finite-horizon collapse across real-data quotas, rare prevalences, and feedback perturbations via exhaustive multi-generation chains is computationally prohibitive. We develop a decoupled framework that forecasts multi-generation collapse probabilities and locates operating risk boundaries from independent single-generation conditional fits alone. Pairing an exact three-source multinomial count law with single-generation response banks propagates count marginals in closed form, backed by explicit calibration-error and boundary-resolution bounds. For additive Gaussian perturbations, we further prove that equal-variance all-row and sparse policies reverse their boundary-crossing order at a unique hyperplane distance. Across a 2,178-setting count benchmark, exact propagation cuts risk mean absolute error (MAE) from 1.85 to 0.49 percentage points (pp). Across ten two-dimensional learners, calibration achieves 2.60--5.69~pp six-round core MAE on nine stationary learners (65--81\% below an unperturbed baseline), diagnoses non-stationary outlier drift in standard DDIM (16.38~pp) via a stability probe, and resolves the predicted six-round geometric reversal. On Fashion-MNIST latent flow-matching chains, calibration outperforms direct-chain Gaussian-process interpolation at lower fit budgets and tracks the 20\% latent-perturbation boundary shift (3.14 versus 10.78~pp MAE for proportion copying) driven by opposing inflow to the rare region and outflow from its core.

history.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock
history.summary: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.

history.title: AeroJEPA: A Two-Stage Framework for Aerosol Forecasting with Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
history.summary: Aerosol forecasting requires integrating sparse ground observations and modeling meteorologically driven concentration evolution and spatial structure. However, analysis-initialized forecasts make limited explicit use of historical observations, while pointwise regression tends to smooth local variations and provides limited constraints on fine spatial structures. In this work, we propose AeroJEPA, a two-stage joint-embedding predictive framework for regional surface PM$_{2.5}$ forecasting. Specifically, Stage I fuses historical observations, model backgrounds, and meteorological information to predict an initial future state, meteorological conditions, and multi-scale structures. Morphology-guided encoding and joint-embedding predictive supervision support learning future spatial representations, supplementing concentration regression with structural constraints. Stage II uses predicted meteorology to guide state refinement and incorporates coarse- and fine-scale structures into state updates and decoding to generate the concentration field at a single future time step. Experiments show that AeroJEPA reduces gridded and independent-station RMSE by 17.23\% and 7.90\%, respectively, relative to PFGNet, while improving spatial consistency with analysis fields. In a 48 h recursive forecasting case study, AeroJEPA generally achieves lower RMSE and MAE than the numerical forecasts across the forecast period, indicating promising short- to medium-range forecasting performance.
